reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A smoking-related interstitial lung disease occurring almost exclusively in current or heavy former smokers.
Forms part of a spectrum with desquamative interstitial pneumonia; asymptomatic respiratory bronchiolitis is a common incidental finding in smokers, whereas RB-ILD is the symptomatic form.
Presents with mild breathlessness and cough; crackles may be present but finger clubbing is uncommon.
HRCT shows centrilobular nodules, patchy ground-glass opacity and bronchial wall thickening, often upper-zone predominant, together with centrilobular emphysema.
Histology demonstrates pigmented 'smoker's' macrophages accumulating within respiratory bronchioles and surrounding alveoli with mild peribronchiolar fibrosis.
Bronchoalveolar lavage shows characteristic golden-brown pigmented macrophages.
Smoking cessation is the cornerstone of management and may lead to stabilisation or improvement.
Corticosteroids are reserved for progressive disease, where the supporting evidence is limited.
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic inhalation of cigarette smoke provokes accumulation of pigment-laden macrophages within respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spaces, accompanied by mild bronchiolocentric inflammation and fibrosis. This bronchiolocentric distribution and the strong causal link to tobacco distinguish RB-ILD from the more diffuse alveolar macrophage filling of desquamative interstitial pneumonia, with which it overlaps.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema
Early or subclinical idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
additionalInvestigations: Detailed smoking history and HRCT thorax
Pulmonary function tests, which may show a mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern with reduced transfer factor
Exclusion of hypersensitivity pneumonitis with precipitins and exposure history
Surgical lung biopsy only if the diagnosis remains unclear after multidisciplinary review
redFlags: Progressive decline despite smoking cessation, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Development of honeycombing suggesting an alternative fibrotic interstitial lung disease
Radiological features raising concern for Langerhans cell histiocytosis or malignancy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally favourable, particularly with smoking cessation; most patients stabilise, although some have persistent symptoms and a minority progress.
pitfalls: Diagnosing RB-ILD in a lifelong non-smoker without reconsidering the diagnosis
Not prioritising smoking cessation as the primary therapy
Confusing incidental respiratory bronchiolitis with symptomatic RB-ILD
Overtreating with immunosuppression when smoking cessation would suffice
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
ATS/ERS international multidisciplinary classification of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
management: Prioritise complete smoking cessation with nicotine replacement or pharmacotherapy, as it is the primary and most effective intervention
Reserve a trial of corticosteroids for symptomatic or progressive disease persisting after stopping smoking
Add pulmonary rehabilitation, ambulatory oxygen for exertional hypoxaemia, and routine vaccination
Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests including transfer factor and interval HRCT to detect progression
Manage coexisting centrilobular emphysema and other smoking-related disease concurrently
Review within an interstitial lung disease multidisciplinary team, escalating to lung biopsy only if the diagnosis becomes unclear
